consensus_summary: Hate is context-dependent: primarily a Semitic idiom for comparative preference (‘love less’), renunciation of claim, or decisive rejection/non-election in favor of another loyalty (discipleship and election texts); secondarily, sinful interpersonal enmity as the moral opposite of love; also righteous abhorrence of evil, divine judicial opposition, and the world’s hostility to Christ/believers.
book_summary: Hate means to un-choose—to repudiate a covenant partner or claim in favor of another—enacted by refusal, disfavor, or sending away, not merely feelings of hostility; opposite of love.
consensus_core_identification: Comparative preference or decisive rejection/renunciation of a rival claim or allegiance (glossed as ‘love less’), distinct from raw malice in key texts; also moral opposite of love.
book_core_identification: To un-choose / repudiate a covenant partner or claim in favor of another, enacted through refusal, disfavor, or sending away.
boundary_disagreement: Book requires active un-choosing/repudiation of a covenant partner or claim and demotes mere emotion or the ‘love less’ softening; consensus admits broader cases of emotional hostility, hyperbolic preference, righteous hatred of evil, and plain ethical enmity without requiring covenantal un-choosing language.
material_contradiction: None; book selects and sharpens the consensus’s idiomatic-rejection strand rather than replacing its referent.
rationale: Minimum cores align on repudiation/rejection in favor of another rather than raw feeling. Consensus (esp. A/B primary and C/D alternatives) already centers the Semitic idiom of renouncing claim or loving less (Luke 14:26, Gen 29, election texts). Book preserves that referent but narrows precision and extension to ‘un-choose’ a covenant partner/claim, enacted outwardly, explicitly distancing from the emotion-or-‘love-less’ common view it notes. This is boundary refinement (cases of pure hostility or non-covenantal abhorrence are sidelined), not core replacement or novelty.
strongest_objection: Consensus treats hate as polyvalent, with a dominant ethical sense (hatred of persons = darkness/murder, opposite agape) that a single ‘un-choose’ definition may under-emphasize or reframe too uniformly.
